course.learn: A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a hardware-based security component that can securely generate/store cryptographic material and measure platform integrity.
course.why: Keeping key material in dedicated hardware makes it harder for malware to steal secrets directly from normal system storage.
course.example: Full-disk encryption seals a key to the TPM so the drive unlocks only when expected boot measurements are present.
course.exam: TPM is typically built into an endpoint/platform; HSM is usually a stronger dedicated device/service for protecting high-value keys at scale.

defs: Transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand it.

course.learn: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a dedicated tamper-resistant device or service for generating, storing, and performing cryptographic operations with high-value keys.
course.why: HSMs reduce the chance that private keys can be exported or stolen from general-purpose systems.
course.example: A certificate authority keeps its signing key inside an HSM and performs signing operations without exposing the private key to the host OS.
course.exam: HSM = dedicated high-assurance key protection; TPM = platform-integrated endpoint trust/key storage.

course.learn: Key-management systems centralize the creation, storage, rotation, access, backup, and retirement of cryptographic keys. Key escrow stores a recoverable copy under controlled conditions.
course.why: Losing an encryption key can make legitimate data permanently inaccessible, while leaking the key destroys confidentiality.
course.example: A cloud KMS rotates database-encryption keys automatically and restricts key use to a specific application role.
course.exam: CompTIA may test availability versus confidentiality tradeoffs. Escrow improves recoverability but creates a high-value secret that must be strongly protected.

defs: Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

course.learn: A secure enclave is an isolated execution area designed to protect sensitive computations and secrets even if the main operating system is compromised.
course.why: Isolation reduces the number of components that can directly access high-value secrets.
course.example: A mobile device stores biometric-processing keys inside a hardware-backed enclave instead of normal application memory.
course.exam: Look for isolated protected processing or protected key material on a device.

breakdown.explanation: Hardware security risk includes vulnerable firmware, malicious peripherals, insecure interfaces, unsupported devices, and physical tampering.
Isolation separates a risky or sensitive system from other resources so compromise cannot easily spread. Physical isolation and air gaps provide stronger separation than ordinary logical controls.
